sources.title: Norsk Folkemuseum, Norway at a crossroads in 1905
sources.note: Factories, cities, labor organization and social differences grew at the end of the nineteenth century.

sources.title: Norsk Folkemuseum, Hygiene
sources.note: Water heating made washing laborious; bathhouses, outdoor privies and rare early water closets.

sources.title: Norsk Folkemuseum, Østerdalen
sources.note: Mid-nineteenth-century farm toilets were uncommon in parts of rural Norway; many relieved themselves outdoors.

sources.title: Stockholmskällan, Wells, privies and drains
sources.note: Stockholm relied on courtyard dry privies; dirty wells spread disease; water closets remained rare in 1895.

sources.title: Public Health Agency of Sweden, Previous vaccination programmes
sources.note: Swedish smallpox vaccination began in the early nineteenth century.

sources.title: Government of Norway, Norwegianization in schools
sources.note: Norwegian policy pressed Sami children to learn Norwegian and restricted Sami language in schools during the union era.

sources.title: Nordiska museet, Migration in nineteenth-century Sweden
sources.note: Land shortages and economic hardship sent many Swedish people toward America.

The imported “sweden-norway” record spans approximately 1815 to 1914; the historical union lasted 1814 to 1905. Norway and Sweden retained distinct institutions. Imported polygon accuracy is unverified.

Daily-life examples are from particular Norwegian and Swedish households, not uniform across class, language and place. Norwegianization harmed Sami and Kven communities. Narrative awaits independent review.

aliases: United Kingdoms of Sweden and Norway
proposedOverrides.summary: Sweden and Norway shared a monarch from 1814 to 1905, while Norway retained its own constitution and parliament. The imported “sweden-norway” map interval runs from about 1815 to 1914, but the union ended in 1905. Households ranged from farms to growing towns; children helped with chores, schooling expanded unevenly, and disease and sanitation remained everyday concerns. Norwegian parliamentarianism, language and cultural movements, and disputes over foreign affairs shaped the end of the union. Sami people faced coercive language policy. Norway and Sweden separated through negotiation in 1905.
